Pricing and features were accurate at the time of writing.Key Takeaways Sonnet 4.6 is the best value-per-dollar coding model in 2026: At $3/$15 per million tokens with 79.6% SWE-bench Verified, it delivers 95%+ of GPT-5.4's coding quality at a fraction of the cost. GPT-5.4 wins on raw capability but costs more in practice: GPT-5.4 leads SWE-bench Pro (57.7%) and Terminal-Bench (75.1%), but its pricing doubles beyond 272K tokens and reasoning mode adds overhead. Sonnet is 2-3x faster for code generation: At 44-63 tokens/sec versus GPT-5.4's typical 20-30 t/s, Sonnet lets you iterate faster on everyday coding tasks. The smart strategy is using both: Sonnet 4.6 as your default for speed and cost, GPT-5.4 when you need maximum reasoning depth or computer use capabilities. For most developers, Sonnet 4.6 is the right starting point: Unless your work regularly involves complex multi-step autonomous coding, Sonnet handles it. Claude Sonnet 4.6 vs GPT-5.4: Which AI Model for Coding? We already covered GPT-5.4 vs Claude Opus 4.6 -- the frontier heavyweights. But most developers are not paying Opus prices every day. The real question is this: should your daily driver be Claude Sonnet 4.6 or GPT-5.4? These are the two models that most developers actually use for coding. Sonnet 4.6 (released February 17, 2026) is Anthropic's mid-tier model that punches well above its weight. GPT-5.4 (released March 5, 2026) is OpenAI's unified reasoning model that combines coding, computer use, and knowledge work in one package. One is cheaper and faster. The other is more capable on hard problems. Here is exactly how they compare, with real numbers. The Real Question Stop asking "which model is better." That framing wastes your time. Both models can write a React component, debug a Python script, or generate SQL queries. For 80% of daily coding tasks, the output quality is indistinguishable. The real question is: which model gives you the best results per dollar and per second for YOUR specific work? If you write boilerplate, fix bugs, and iterate on features all day, speed and cost dominate. If you architect complex systems, debug gnarly multi-file issues, or run autonomous coding agents, raw capability matters more. This comparison will help you decide where each model fits in your workflow. Benchmark Comparison Head-to-Head Coding Scores BenchmarkSonnet 4.6GPT-5.4WinnerSWE-bench Verified79.6%~80% (77.2% thinking)GPT-5.4 (marginal)SWE-bench Pro~47%57.7%GPT-5.4Terminal-Bench 2.059.1%75.1%GPT-5.4OSWorld (Computer Use)72.5%75%GPT-5.4HumanEval+~94%~95%TieMMLU Pro~82%~84%GPT-5.4 (marginal) What the Numbers Actually Mean SWE-bench Verified is nearly a tie. Sonnet 4.6 at 79.6% versus GPT-5.4 at roughly 80% -- that 0.4% gap is within noise for real-world coding. Both models can resolve the same class of GitHub issues with high reliability. SWE-bench Pro tells a different story. This harder variant, designed to resist benchmark gaming, shows GPT-5.4 at 57.7% versus Sonnet's estimated 47%. That is a meaningful gap on genuinely novel engineering problems. Terminal-Bench 2.0 is where GPT-5.4 pulls away dramatically. At 75.1% versus 59.1%, GPT-5.4 is substantially better at autonomous terminal-based coding -- file editing, git operations, build systems, debugging loops. If you run agentic coding workflows, this gap matters. The bottom line: for standard coding tasks (the kind measured by SWE-bench Verified), they are practically equal. For hard, autonomous, multi-step problems, GPT-5.4 has a clear edge. Speed Comparison Speed matters for coding. Every second you wait for a completion is a second your flow state degrades. MetricSonnet 4.6GPT-5.4Output speed (standard)44 tokens/sec~20-25 tokens/secOutput speed (max effort)63 tokens/sec~15-20 tokens/secTime to first token~1.2 sec~2-3 secTypical inline completion0.5-1.5 sec1.5-3 secFull function generation2-4 sec4-8 secComplex refactoring (500 lines)8-15 sec15-30 sec Sonnet 4.6 is roughly 2-3x faster for code generation across the board. This is not a marginal difference. When you are iterating on code -- write, test, adjust, repeat -- those seconds compound into minutes per hour. For inline completions in editors like Cursor or VS Code, Sonnet's speed advantage is especially noticeable. The model responds fast enough to feel like autocomplete rather than a query-and-wait interaction. GPT-5.4's slower speed is partly because it routes through reasoning by default. You are paying for thinking time even on simple completions. That reasoning overhead buys you better results on hard problems but slows you down on easy ones.
